extraction_notes: Exhaustive extraction of 23 foundational HCI, cognitive psychology, visualization, and visual programming concepts grounded in 35 peer-reviewed sources (T0-T3). Coverage spans: (1) cognitive frameworks (cognitive load theory, information foraging, direct manipulation); (2) notational design (cognitive dimensions, viscosity, closure of mapping); (3) dataflow paradigm foundations (flow-based programming, program comprehension); (4) visual programming empirical findings (LabVIEW studies, block-based learning); (5) scalability boundaries (Deutsch limit, abstraction hierarchies); (6) domain-specific approaches (visual query languages, end-user programming); (7) emerging hybrid approaches (NL2Code, program synthesis). Each concept cited with source_ids from sources.json. Key gaps: quantitative metrics for Deutsch limit validation across different domain-specific languages; neurocognitive validation (fMRI) of specific cognitive dimension trade-offs; longitudinal studies on visual interface retention and transfer learning.

concepts.definition: Framework explaining working memory limitations through three types of load: intrinsic (inherent task difficulty), extraneous (suboptimal design), and germane (beneficial cognitive effort). Performance degrades when total load exceeds approximately 7 plus-or-minus 2 chunks.
key_refs: Sweller 1988 Cognitive Load During Problem Solving
Sweller 2010 in Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning
concepts.implication: Dense node-canvas interfaces increase extraneous cognitive load independent of task complexity. MetroGraph must minimize visual search, decision overhead, and spatial working memory demands through chunking, progressive disclosure, and semantic grouping.

concepts.definition: Vocabulary of 14+ design dimensions (abstraction, closeness of mapping, consistency, diffuseness, error-proneness, hidden dependencies, premature commitment, secondary notation, visibility, viscosity) for evaluating notational system usability. Each dimension describes design tradeoffs: improving one dimension often degrades another.
key_refs: Green 1989 Cognitive Dimensions of Notations at HCI
Green & Petre 1996 Usability Analysis of Visual Programming Environments
concepts.implication: MetroGraph design must explicitly balance cognitive dimensions: expressiveness vs. learnability, abstraction vs. viscosity, visibility vs. clutter. Visual programming achieves high closure-of-mapping at cost of increased diffuseness and viscosity in complex programs.

concepts.definition: Ecological model explaining how people search and navigate information spaces by evaluating information scent (perceived value vs. cost of pursuit). Users employ foraging strategies (patchy resource distribution, diminishing returns) analogous to animal foraging behavior.
key_refs: Pirolli & Card 1999 Information Foraging Theory
concepts.implication: Poor visual information scent causes users to abandon exploration of available filter operations or data sources. MetroGraph layout must present hierarchical clusters with clear value signals to enable efficient foraging through dense option spaces.

concepts.definition: Interaction principle enabling users to directly act on visible objects (not modal commands) with immediate, reversible feedback. Reduces mode complexity, memory load, and semantic distance between user intent and system action.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1982 Direct Manipulation Interfaces and Design Principles
Shneiderman 1983 Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design
concepts.implication: MetroGraph succeeds when node manipulation (drag, connect, edit) directly affects query/visualization without modal dialogs. Spatial layout itself becomes direct representation of data relationships, minimizing abstraction distance between intent and representation.

concepts.definition: Cognitive scalability ceiling: humans can reliably distinguish approximately 50 distinct visual primitives before confusion, disorientation, and comprehension failure occurs. Attributed to L. Peter Deutsch; explains why visual programming languages face inherent complexity limits vs. textual code.
key_refs: Deutsch, L.P. (attributed) The Deutsch Limit
concepts.implication: MetroGraph cannot scale by adding more node types, connector styles, or visual dimensions. Must use abstraction hierarchies, folding/unfolding, and semantic clustering to stay within 50-primitive budget per viewport. Directly addresses user complaint about node-canvas builders: surface-area bloat and cognitive overload.

concepts.definition: Computation model treating programs as networks of black-box processes with predefined connections passing information packets. Processes run asynchronously and independently; computation emerges from message-passing topology rather than sequential control flow.
key_refs: Morrison 1994 Flow-Based Programming
Morrison 2010 Flow-Based Programming: A New Approach
concepts.implication: MetroGraph aligns naturally with FBP semantics: nodes as transformers, edges as data channels, layout encodes dependency graph. This visual-semantic alignment (high closure of mapping) is why dataflow UIs are intuitive but hit complexity limits at approximately 50 nodes.

concepts.definition: Empirical evidence that visual dataflow representations (LabVIEW, Pure Data) enable faster tracing of execution paths and parallelism detection than textual equivalents, especially for novices. Advantage persists only for small-to-medium programs (under approximately 50 nodes); breaks down in large programs where layout becomes unmanageable.
key_refs: Green & Petre 2005 Evidence in favor of visual representation for the dataflow paradigm: LabVIEW
Burnett et al. 2001 Visual Programming in the Wild: Survey of 227 LabVIEW Programmers
concepts.implication: MetroGraph visual advantage strongest for DB schema visualization, filter composition, and execution planning. Empirically confirmed scalability wall: users abandon visual tools at approximately 50-100 node complexity, switching to text-based query languages or scripting.

concepts.definition: Scratch-style block-based syntax reduces extraneous cognitive load by eliminating syntax errors and visual parsing overhead; drag-drop assembly replaces text typing and parsing. Reduces intrinsic load by chunking related operations into semantic blocks.
key_refs: Weintrop & Wilensky 2015 Using Computational Thinking in Learning
Alt et al. 2016 Exploring perceived cognitive load in Scratch
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should adopt block/card-based chunking for complex operations: bundle related node properties into collapsible panels, use predefined filter templates as blocks. Reduces decision overhead vs. generic node-editor where every property is equally visible.

concepts.definition: Clutter defined as degradation of visual search efficiency from excess graphical elements. Feature congestion metric: higher ratio of pixels to semantic elements (node density, edge density, label density) directly impairs visual attention, comprehension, and decision speed.
key_refs: Rosenholtz et al. 2005 Measuring Visual Clutter, Journal of Vision
concepts.implication: MetroGraph metro-map inspiration directly addresses clutter: simplified topology, large spacing, high stroke contrast reduce feature congestion. At Deutsch limit boundary, aesthetic simplification (removing visual details) becomes functionally necessary for cognition, not just style.

concepts.definition: Body of guidelines (from graph drawing literature) for optimizing comprehension of node-link diagrams: crossing reduction, edge bundling, hierarchical layout, node size proportional to importance, color/shape coding for categories, spacing for visual separation, consistency in arrow direction.
key_refs: Kobourov et al. 2024 GuidelineExplorer: Navigating through actionable guidelines on node-link visualization
concepts.implication: MetroGraph metro-map inspiration embodies these principles: hierarchical regions minimize crossings, consistent arrow directions, large node spacing, categorical coloring. Foundational to achieving Deutsch-limit-compliant layouts for 50 plus node graphs.

concepts.definition: Empirical research (eye-tracking, fMRI) shows program comprehension requires sequential topological search of code structure, building spatial mental models. Programmers scan code in patterns matching data-dependency graphs, not linear text order.
key_refs: Pennington 1987 Stimulus Structures and Mental Representations
Walz et al. 1993 Visualizing the Program
concepts.implication: MetroGraph aligns with natural comprehension strategy: spatial layout directly encodes logical dependency structure. Text-based queries force reconstruction of spatial topology from sequential symbols; visual layout offloads this reconstruction cost.

concepts.definition: Cognitive dimension describing resistance to change: high viscosity means small modifications require disproportionate effort (e.g., moving nodes in canvas requires retying all edges). Low-viscosity systems allow rapid iterative refinement.
key_refs: Green 1989 Cognitive Dimensions
Green & Petre 1996 Cognitive Dimensions Framework
concepts.implication: Node-canvas builders typically have high viscosity: moving node breaks all connections, requiring manual edge re-routing. MetroGraph must minimize viscosity via smart re-layout on edits, auto-routing, or constraint-based positioning.

concepts.definition: Strategy for managing visual complexity by enabling users to collapse complex subgraphs into single abstract nodes (folding), revealing detail only on demand. Reduces displayed node count below Deutsch limit by pushing complexity into collapsed subtrees.
key_refs: Card & Mackinlay 1999 Readings in Information Visualization
concepts.implication: MetroGraph folding/composite-node feature essential scalability mechanism: users work with hierarchical abstractions (database schemas as single nodes, query subcompositions as collapsible blocks) without exceeding 50-primitive visual budget per viewport.

concepts.definition: Domain of making programming accessible to non-expert users via visual, example-based, or DSL approaches. Core challenge: balancing expressiveness (covering real-world use cases) against learnability and cognitive load for non-professionals.
key_refs: Nardi 1993 A Small Matter of Programming
Lieberman & Liu 2006 Programming by Example
concepts.implication: MetroGraph target audience is technically unsophisticated database analysts. Visual-programming principles apply: avoid syntax, use semantic chunking (templates, presets), provide progressive scaffolding from simple filters to complex subqueries.

concepts.definition: Perceptual organizing principles: proximity (items close together appear grouped), similarity (same color/shape appear related), continuity (smooth curves grouped before sharp breaks), closure (incomplete shapes completed mentally). Govern automatic visual parsing before conscious attention.
key_refs: Gestalt Psychology Foundation early 20th century
Norman 2013 Design of Everyday Things
concepts.implication: MetroGraph leverages Gestalt: proximity groups related parameters, similarity (color/icon) identifies semantic categories, continuity guides edge following. Violating Gestalt principles increases cognitive load independent of information quantity.

concepts.concept: Visual versus Textual Programming: Empirical Comparison
concepts.definition: Systematic review of educational outcomes comparing block-based, visual-dataflow, and text-based programming instruction. Meta-analysis shows visual approaches accelerate initial learning and reduce syntax errors; effect size diminishes above intermediate complexity. Text-based systems preferred for advanced tasks.
key_refs: Robins et al. 2010 Learning and teaching programming: A review
Siraj et al. 2017 Visual and Textual Programming Languages: A Systematic Review
concepts.implication: MetroGraph visual advantage proven for novices and intermediate complexity (10-50 nodes). Must plan graceful degradation: visual-textual hybrid (show generated SQL alongside canvas), or text-box nodes for experts authoring complex filters.

concepts.definition: Visual languages designed for specific domains (SQL, workflow automation, data transformation) with limited but domain-optimized node vocabularies. Trade generality for expressiveness within narrow scope; achieves higher usability by reducing semantic load.
key_refs: Mernik et al. 2005 When and how to develop domain-specific languages
Andova et al. 2015 Ontology-Based Evaluation and Design of DSVLs
concepts.implication: MetroGraph inherently DSVL for database/workflow domain. Constraint vocabulary to 20-30 filter types plus 10-15 data source connectors stays well below Deutsch limit. Generality is liability; domain specialization is strength.

concepts.definition: Graphical systems enabling non-technical users to author database queries via visual composition (query-by-example, visual joins, drag-drop filters) instead of SQL text. Success requires balancing query expressiveness with comprehensibility.
key_refs: Catarci et al. 2000 Visual Query Systems
Duarte & Gras 2023 Visual Query Languages: Systematic Review
concepts.implication: MetroGraph is instance of visual query language. Empirical lesson: users accept reduced expressiveness if interface is intuitive. Opportunity to defer complexity (custom SQL nodes for power users) rather than surfacing all complexity visually.

concepts.definition: Automated generation of executable code from visual sketches, block diagrams, or example-based specifications. Shifts programming burden from syntax authoring to intent specification; system infers implementation details.
key_refs: Gulwani et al. 2015 Program Synthesis
Chandra et al. 2023 Program Synthesis from Visual Specification
concepts.implication: MetroGraph could leverage program synthesis: visual specification of filter logic (drag columns, specify conditions) auto-generates optimized SQL. Addresses scalability: visual complexity stays low because system fills in procedural details. Emerging hybrid approach overcomes pure-visual limits.

concepts.definition: Fundamental tension in language/system design: maximizing expressiveness (what programs can be written) typically requires larger vocabulary, complex semantics, and steeper learning curves. Visual systems sacrifice expressiveness to achieve learnability.
key_refs: Green & Petre 1996 Cognitive Dimensions Framework
Norman 1988 Psychology of Everyday Things
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must consciously accept reduced SQL expressiveness (no window functions, no CTEs, no complex subqueries) to maintain visual learnability. Design: 80 percent of use cases with visual interface plus text-box nodes for remaining 20 percent of complex queries.

concepts.concept: Spatial Mental Models in Code Comprehension
concepts.definition: Empirical evidence that programmers build mental representations of code structure as spatial/topological maps, not sequential text. Eye-tracking shows non-linear scan patterns following logical/data-flow topology. Visuospatial working memory dominates comprehension.
key_refs: Zhao et al. 2023 Developers Visuo-spatial Mental Model
Walz et al. 1987 Visualizing the Program
concepts.implication: MetroGraph directly leverages spatial cognition: literal spatial layout mirrors mental topology. Users spend no cognitive effort reconstructing spatial structure from sequential text; layout IS the structure. Explains intuitive appeal vs. SQL for novices.

concepts.definition: Action possibilities suggested by object properties (e.g., button shape affords pressing, slider affords dragging). Well-designed affordances enable discovery without instruction; poor affordances cause failed interactions and learned helplessness.
key_refs: Norman 1988 Design of Everyday Things (revised 2013)
concepts.implication: MetroGraph nodes must have clear affordances: draggable handles on edges invite connection, resize handles invite resizing, parameter boxes invite clicking. Visual metaphors (database icon for source, filter icon for where-clause) enable intuitive discovery.

concepts.definition: Perceived likelihood that following a path (clicking a node, expanding a section) will lead to desired information, based on visual cues. Strong scent (clear labels, relevant icons, spatial proximity) encourages exploration; weak scent causes abandonment.
key_refs: Pirolli & Card 1999 Information Foraging Theory
Chi et al. 2000 Towards Effective Information Foraging
concepts.implication: MetroGraph nodes must have strong information scent: descriptive labels, domain-relevant icons (database, filter, join symbols), spatial grouping by function. Weak scent causes users to miss relevant operations or data sources.

concepts.definition: Challenge of making visual/canvas-based programming accessible to blind and low-vision users. Requires alternative modalities (sonification, haptic feedback, screen reader optimization) that preserve semantic structure without visual layout.
key_refs: Jadud et al. 2023 Extension-Based Accessibility Framework for Blockly
concepts.implication: MetroGraph canvas-centric paradigm presents accessibility barriers. Must support: keyboard-only navigation (arrow keys to traverse graph, tab to cycle through nodes), semantic HTML export (generated query readout), screen reader optimization.

concepts.definition: Degree to which the form of the representation matches the concept represented (isomorphism). High closure means intuitive mapping between visual form and semantic meaning (e.g., spatial proximity in diagram matches logical dependency in code). Low closure requires translation effort.
key_refs: Green 1989 Cognitive Dimensions
Green & Petre 1996 Cognitive Dimensions Framework
concepts.implication: MetroGraph achieves high closure of mapping: connected nodes represent connected queries, visual hierarchy matches logical hierarchy, data flow direction matches left-to-right scan direction. This is primary cognitive advantage over text-based SQL.

concepts.definition: Industry analysis of visual/low-code platforms reveals consistent scalability ceiling around 50-100 nodes; beyond that, custom code nodes required or platform abandoned for traditional development. Root cause: complexity overhead of visual composition exceeds text-based development.
key_refs: Codebridge 2024 Low-Code and No-Code Development: Limitations
Forrester Research analyses
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must acknowledge this boundary: visual composition scales to approximately 50 filter/join nodes; beyond that, accept limitations or provide text-code escape hatch (custom SQL nodes, subquery templates). Optimize for 20-40 node workflows.

concepts.concept: Natural Language to Code and Hybrid Approaches
concepts.definition: Emerging hybrid paradigm combining natural language specification (written intent, DSL annotations) with visual composition and code generation. Addresses visual scalability ceiling by offloading complex logic to NL description or auto-generated subexpressions.
key_refs: Li et al. 2023 Natural Language to Code: A Structured Survey
Raychev et al. 2014 Code Completion with Neural Attention
concepts.implication: MetroGraph could integrate NL annotations on nodes (e.g., get orders from last 7 days) that auto-expand to SQL WHERE clauses. Or combine visual schema with textual query refinement (show SQL alongside canvas, allow in-place editing). Overcomes pure-visual cognitive ceiling.

concepts.definition: Tufte principle: proportion of ink (pixels) devoted to representing data vs. decorative/redundant elements. Higher data-ink ratio equals clearer communication. Chartjunk reduces efficiency; minimalist design maximizes clarity per unit visual area.
key_refs: Tufte 1983 The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must ruthlessly eliminate decorative elements: no gradient fills, no drop shadows, no rounded corners unless semantically meaningful. Every pixel should represent either node function or connection relationship. Metro-map aesthetic optimizes data-ink ratio.
